## 1. Summary

<!--# 
With a maximum of 300 words, describe the indicator in general terms as you would to a non-expert. Think of this as a kind of common language summary. Follow the four numbers sub-headers below. under point 2, it is possible under  include a bullet point list of the specific steps in the workflow. 
 -->
The natural pattern of river water flow in most parts of Scandinavia is low flow during winter, when most precipitation comes in the form of snow, and with a flood peak during spring and early summer when the snow melts. Hydropower development involving large water reservoirs affects this pattern, typically by increasing the water flow during winter and decreasing water flow during spring and early summer. This indicator uses measurements of water flow from NVE's stations during the last 20 years and compares it with estimates of natural water flow at the same locations, using NVE'S NEVINA model tool.

## 2. About the underlying data

<!--# Give a general introduction the datasets you have used, and provide more specific details in the sub-chapters.  -->  

There are two main datasets of underlaying data:

1) Measured low-flow indices and flood values for rivers (at the posiotion of river flow measurement stations)
Low-flow indices was set to the 5% percentile of water flow during the winter months (1. October-30. April) in both cases.

2) Estimated low-flow indices and flood values for rivers (at the posiotion of river flow measurement stations) if the upstream river catchment was unaffected by hydropower development. The estimates were found using NEVINA, which calculates catchment boundaries and catchment characteristics based on natural watershed boundaries. This means that existing regulations, reservoirs, or other hydrological alterations within the catchment are not taken into account. All catchment characteristics, low-flow indices, and flood values are calculated automatically. The estimates are based on the observed climate in the period 1991-2020.

<!--# Describe the rationale for assigning the indicator to the ECT class. See https://oneecosystem.pensoft.net/article/58218/

The indicator is assigned to "A1 - Physical state characteristics" as it relates to extremes of water flow, which affects the physical effects of river and river-related habitats. For instance, with decreasing floods, sand banks along the rivers become colonised  by plants and sand banks no longer functions as a habitat for specialised, red-listed species.

## 5. Uncertainties
### 5.1 General uncertainties
<!--# Describe the main reasons why you might not trust 100% the final value to represent the given ecosystem characteristic for the give ecosystem type. What aspects of this condition metric are most sensitive to subjective decitions? Is the spatial sampling sufficient? Does the choice of modeling framework affect the values? Is the metric relevant do describe ecosystem condition for the give ecosystem type?  -->

The mathematical model used in NEVINA is based on the runoff map for the 1961-1990 period. We have used the runoff map for 1991-2020 as input to this model, but as the model itself has not been updated, this constitutes a source of error and possibly also an unknown bias.

### 7.2 Estimated flood and low-water values for natural watershed

These are estimates of the mean flood (highest daily water flow over a year) and low-water values (5% percentiles) of water flow through the winter (1. October-30. April), esimated using the NEVINA tool offered by NVE (nevina.nve.no),  For mean flood, we used the estimates based on "Regional flomfrekvensanalyse" (RFFA-2018).  Is input, we used the observed meteorological data (precipitation, snow, temperature, etc.) for the 30-year period 1991-2020. 

```{r read_nevina_results}  

stations_orig <- read_seriestasjoner("../data/seriestasjoner.csv")

head(stations_orig, 3) |> kable(caption = "Data sample (three stations)")  

```

### 7.3. Watershed metadata    

These data was downloaded from seriekart.nve.no and contains a large number of variables for the catchment of each measurement station. The most interesting ones for our analysis are the indices of hydropower regulation and hydropower dams, which both on scale 0-1 and indicate how much of the catchment  that is affected by hydropower regulation (including run-of-river hydro power stations) and hydropower regulation dams ("Reguleringsgrad magasin"). We focused on the latter, hereby called **dam index**. For many stations these indices are small or zero, but they mostly have quite small catchments.  

```{r read_metadata}  

# add degree of hydropower dams to the station data

# all metadata 
stations_meta <- readr::read_csv("../data/seriestasjoner_meta.csv", col_types = columntypes_meta, na = c("NA", "Ikke angitt"))

# spec(stations_meta)
# names(stations_meta)

# we pick degree of hydropower dams, change column name, and add that column to 'stations_orig'  

stations_meta <- stations_meta |> 
  rename(
    steepness = `Bratthet (1085-gradient, m/km)`,
    perc_bogs = Myrprosent,
    perc_lake = `Effektiv sjøprosent`,
    perc_agri = Jordbruksprosent,
    perc_forest = Skogprosent,
    perc_mount = Snaufjellprosent,
    perc_glacier = Breprosent,
    river_gradient = `Elvegradient (m/km)`,
    river_length = `Elvelengde (km)`,
    river_density = `Elvetetthet (m/km)`,
    alti_med = `Medianhøyde (m)`,
    alti_10p = `Høyde 10 persentil (m)`,
    alti_90p = `Høyde 90 persentil (m)`,
    altitude = `Høyde over havet (m)`,
    index_regul = `Reguleringsgrad areal`,
    index_dams = `Reguleringsgrad mag,`
  )

stations_orig2 <- merge(stations_orig, stations_meta, by =  "stasjonsnr") 

# all metadata 
stations <- stations_orig2 |> 
  filter(!is.na(areal_km2) & !is.na(index_dams))

gg1 <- ggplot(stations, aes(x = areal_km2, y = index_dams)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Catchment area (km2)", y = "Hydropower dam index")  

gg2 <- ggplot(stations, aes(x = areal_km2, y = index_regul)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Catchment size (km2)", y = "Fraction hydropower regulation (0 - 1)")  

gg3 <- ggplot(stations, aes(x = index_regul, y = index_dams)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Fraction hydropower regulation (0 - 1", y = "Hydropower dam index")  

cowplot::plot_grid(gg1, gg2, gg3, nrow = 1)

```

### 9.1 Calculate observed flow statistics  

For each station and year, we find the annual flood value (maximum  river flow) and the winter low-flow value (the 5% of the months October to April). Then we find the mean and standard deviation of those values for every station. The two are (as expected) highly correlated (figure below). 
```{r, calculate_observed_stats}

# get observed means 
flow_high <- yearly_highflow(dat)
flow_winter <- yearly_lowflow(dat)
flow_statistics <- flow_stats(flow_winter, flow_high)

flow_statistics |> 
  left_join(stations, by = join_by(stasjonsnr)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(highflow_mean, lowflow_mean, fill = areal_km2)) +
         geom_point(shape = 21, size = rel(2)) +
  scale_fill_viridis_b() +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_log10()

```


### 9.2 Indices and indicators  


#### a. Calculate flood index and low-water indicator        

The indices are calculated by comparing the observed statistics of flood and low-water flow with NEVINA's estimates of the same parameters. 
  
For floods, we started by creating a flood index (this index turned out to departure from 1 for rivers without dams, so the flood indicator will therefore be derived later). For river *i*, this is  

$$
\text{Flood\_index}_i
= 1 - \frac{Q_{\text{model,high,i}} - \overline{Q_{\text{obs,high,i}}}}
           {Q_{\text{model,high,i}}}
$$

where $Q_{\text{model,high,i}}$ is the modelled natural flood of river *i* from NEVINA, and $\overline{Q_{\text{obs,high,i}}}$ is the mean of the  observed flood for the same river. 
  combined$lowwater_indicator <- with(combined, 1-(lowflow_mean-lowflow_m3s)/(highflow_mean-lowflow_m3s))
  
The low-water indicator for river *i* depends on the both the modelled natural low-water flow as well as the observed mean flood. If the observed low-water flow is equal to the modelled natural low-water flow, the indicator is 1. If the observed low-water flow is equal to the observed flood flow, the indicator is 0. 

$$
\text{Lowwater\_indicator\}
= 1 - \frac{\overline{Q_{\text{obs,low}}} - Q_{\text{model,low}}}
           {\overline{Q_{\text{obs,high}}} - Q_{\text{model,low}}}
$$

where $Q_{\text{model,low,i}}$ is the modelled mean low water flow of river *i* from NEVINA, and $\overline{Q_{\text{obs,low,i}}}$ is the mean of the  observed low water flow for the same river.  


```{r calculate_indices_1}

# indicator 001: effect of hydropower on floods and low water  
# indicator 002, : effect of hydropower on low water  
dat_indekser_1 <- kalkuler_indikatorer(
  flowstats = flow_statistics, 
  seriestasjoner = stations) |> 
  mutate(log_areal = log10(areal_km2))

gg1 <- ggplot(dat_indekser_1, aes(flood_index)) +
  geom_histogram() +
  scale_x_log10()
gg2 <- ggplot(dat_indekser_1, aes(lowwater_indicator)) +
  geom_histogram() +
```

```{r}
# cut with non-scientific formatting 
cut_noscient <- function(x, breaks){
  # format non-scientific
  breaks_str <- format(breaks, scientific = FALSE)
  # remove extra spaces
  breaks_str <- gsub(" ", "", breaks_str)
  # create labels
  labs <- paste0(
    "(", head(breaks_str, -1),
    ",",
    tail(breaks_str, -1),
    "]"
  )
  cut(x, breaks = breaks, labels = labs)
}
```

### 9.4 Examine observed and modelled water flow  


#### Observed and modelled natural flood values  

In rivers affected, by hydropower, observed values of mean annual flood are expected to lie somewhere below modelled natural flood values.

Figure: Observed values of mean annual flood (y axis, red) and low-water value (y axis, blue) on y axis plotted towards modelled natural flood values (x axis). The line indicates y = x. 
```{r}

ggplot(dat_indekser, 
       aes(highflow_m3s, highflow_mean)) +
  geom_point(shape = 21, size = rel(2), fill = "red") +
  geom_point(aes(y=lowflow_m3s), shape = 21, size = rel(2), fill = "blue2") +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_log10()

```

#### Examine flood indices vs. indices of hydropower  

As shown below (figure a), the index of effect of hydropower on floods varies around 1 for rivers were `index_dams` is zero (i.e. there are no dams in the catchment of the station). As the amount of dams increases, the index goes towards lower numbers. Thus, the flood indices appear to work well. As we see from figure b, `index_regul` (measuring all sorts of hydropower development, including run-of-river hydropower plants that has no large dam) is much less correlated to the flood indicator, indicating that this index is trule closely connected to presence of large dams upstream.


```{r}

# 1. index_dams

mod <- lm(flood_index ~ index_dams, 
          data = dat_indekser |> filter(index_dams > 0), 
          na.action = na.omit)

gg1 <- ggplot(dat_indekser, aes(index_dams, flood_index)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(
    data = dat_indekser |> filter(flood_index > 0),
    method = "lm", linetype = "dashed", color = "red3") +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "Index of hydropower dams", y = "Flood index") +
  labs(subtitle = paste("Model: ", get_model_summ(mod), 
       "\nNote: regression fitted to catchments with dams")) +
  theme(plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 7))

# 2. index_regul

mod <- lm(flood_index ~ index_regul, 
          data = dat_indekser |> filter(index_regul > 0), 
          na.action = na.omit)

gg2 <- ggplot(dat_indekser, aes(index_regul, flood_index)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(
    data = dat_indekser |> filter(index_regul > 0),
    method = "lm", linetype = "dashed", color = "red3") +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "Index of hydropower development", y = "Flood index") +
  labs(subtitle = paste("Model: ", get_model_summ(mod), 
       "\nNote: regression fitted to catchments with hydropower")) +
  theme(plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 7))

plot_grid(gg1, gg2, nrow = 1)

```

### 9.5 Check subsets of data  

```{r}
altitude_limit <- 450
altitude_limit_finnmark <- 200  
normal_riverflow_limit <- 5
```

As the original dataset has many small rivers, as well as river at high altitudes, we decided do focus on relatively low-lying rivers over a certain size. We selected rivers below `r altitude_limit` m altitude, except in Finnmark (which has lower maximum altitude) where we selected rivers below `r altitude_limit_finnmark` m. We also selected only rivers above `r normal_riverflow_limit` m3/second river flow on average.  

#### a. Add groupings  

```{r}
dat_indekser <- dat_indekser |> 
  mutate(
    region = case_when(
      county %in% "Finnmark" ~ "Finnmark",
      county %in% c("Troms", "Finnmark") ~ "Troms og Nordland",
      county %in% c("Trøndelag") ~ "Trøndelag",
      county %in% c("Møre og Romsdal","Vestland","Rogaland") ~ "Vestlandet",
      county %in% c("Agder","Telemark") ~ "Agder og Telemark",
      TRUE ~ "Østlandet"),
    altitude_limit = case_when(
      region %in% "Finnmark" ~ altitude_limit_finnmark,
      TRUE ~ altitude_limit),
    Q_limit = normal_riverflow_limit,
    group1 = case_when(
      altitude < altitude_limit ~ "low",
      altitude >= altitude_limit ~ "high"), 
    group2 = case_when(
      altitude < altitude_limit & normalQ_m3s >= Q_limit ~ "low,big",
      altitude < altitude_limit & normalQ_m3s < Q_limit ~ "low,small",
      altitude >= altitude_limit & normalQ_m3s >= Q_limit ~ "high,big",
      altitude >= altitude_limit & normalQ_m3s < Q_limit ~ "high,small"),
    dams = ifelse(index_dams == 0, "no dams", "dams"),
  )

```

### 9.7 Calculate flood indicator  

We create the final flood indicator based on the flood index. Ideally, the flood index should be 1 for the mean of rivers (within the chosen subset) with no dams in their catchment (reference condition). However, it turns out to be signinficanly higher:
```{r}
mod <- lm(flood_index ~ 1, data = subset(dat_indekser2, dams == "no dams"))
summary(mod)$coef
```

Thus, we create a flood indicator which should be 1 for the mean of rivers (within the chosen subset) with no dams in their catchment (reference condition), and 0 for rivers where the annual flood has been reduced to 20% of the origican flood size, which we take to be no flood in an ecological sense: 

$$
\text{Flood\_indicator}_i
= \frac{Flood\_index_{\text{i}} - 0.2}
           {Flood\_index_{\text{reference}} - 0.2}
$$
where $Flood\_index_{\text{reference}}$ is the mean flood index for rivers with no dams in their catchment.

```{r}

# Reference level 1 = mean for rivers without dams  
ref_1 <- mean(subset(dat_indekser2, dams == "no dams")$flood_index)
ref_0 <- 0.20
```

The $Flood\_index_{\text{reference}}$ was found to be `r ref_1`. 

```{r}

# relatively low-lying rivers over a certain size = data set "dat_indekser2"  


# table(dat_indekser2$dams)
dat_indekser2 <- dat_indekser2 |> 
  mutate(
    flood_indicator = (flood_index - ref_0)/(ref_1 - ref_0),
    dam_weight = ifelse(dams == "dams", 0.7, 0.3)
  )

# check
# mean(subset(dat_indekser2, dams == "no dams")$flood_indicator)
# range(dat_indekser2$flood_indicator)  

```

#### Check the low-water indicator  

We find that the reference level for the low-water indicator is already very close to 1.   

```{r}

# relatively low-lying rivers over a certain size = data set "dat_indekser2"  

# Reference level 1 = mean for rivers without dams  
ref_1 <- mean(subset(dat_indekser2, dams == "no dams")$lowwater_indicator)
ref_1
# ref_1 is already approximately zero  

```



### 9.8 National means  

* Despite having made a subset of dataset with only low-lying rivers, and excluding very small rivers, only 47% of the rivers have dams in their catchment  
* In Norway, approxmately 70% of rivers are affected by hydropower, usually with dams (we were not able to find more exact estimates). Thus, in our sample, we have over-representation of rivers not affected by dams   
* To compensate for the bias of the dataset, we use inverse weighting for the rivers in ours selected subset.  

```{r}
# weights
n_dam <- sum(dat_indekser2$dams == "dams")
n_nodam <- sum(dat_indekser2$dams == "no dams")
n_dam/(n_dam + n_nodam)  # 47% dams
w <- c(0.7/n_dam, 0.3/n_nodam)
w <- w/sum(w)

# table(dat_indekser2$dams)
dat_indekser2 <- dat_indekser2 |> 
  mutate(
    dam_weight = ifelse(dams == "dams", w[1], w[2])
  )

# weighted mean
mod <- lm(flood_indicator ~ 1, dat_indekser2, weights = dam_weight)
summary(mod)

# weighted mean
mod <- lm(lowwater_indicator ~ 1, dat_indekser2, weights = dam_weight)
summary(mod)


```

```{r Appendix_1}
  # read point data for riverflow measurement series (and many, many other point data)
  geo_points_all <- sf::st_read(
    "../../ecRxiv_hydropower_waterflow_test/R/data_observed_waterflow/NVE_seriekart_metadata/NVEKartdata/NVEData.gdb")

  geo_counties <- geo_counties |> 
    mutate(county_area = st_area(geometry)) |> 
    rename(county = navn)
  # set unit to km2 instead of m2 (the number auytomatically changes!)
```
